By Dr. Adrian Leonard Mociulschi —Special for Nine O ’ Clock The opening of a new edition of the George Enescu International Competition offers more than a celebration of talent. It also provides an opportunity to reflect on a mystery that has accompanied music for centuries: why do some creators remain vividly present in human culture long after their own era has vanished? To reflect on this enduring mystery, I turned to Maestro Piotr Borkowski, an internationally acclaimed conductor whose distinguished career has earned him recognition on some of the world’s most prestigious concert stages. Having worked with orchestras and musicians across Europe, Asia, and the Americas, Maestro Borkowski belongs to a rare generation of artists whose experience transcends national and cultural boundaries. In this conversation, he shares his thoughts on the universal power of music, the lasting legacy of George Enescu, and the elusive qualities that allow great works of art to speak to humanity across time. Adrian Leonard Mociulschi: Maestro Borkowski, your career has taken you across many countries, musical traditions, and cultural environments. What common thread have you discovered among musicians around the world and among the great works of the universal repertoire? Piotr Borkowski: For a long time, I never consciously tried to answer that question. The presence of figures such as Bach, Mozart, Beethoven, Chopin, or Enescu in musical history seemed so self-evident that I never felt compelled to reflect upon the phenomenon itself. Yet your question invites deeper consideration. Rather than turning to academic theories, I find myself returning to my own experience. Over several decades, I have had the privilege of working with musicians from Europe, Asia, and the Americas. Gradually, I began to notice something remarkable: regardless of geography, language, culture, or social background, people often respond to certain artistic impulses in strikingly similar ways. Adrian Leonard Mociulschi : How do you explain the fact that musicians trained thousands of miles apart can instinctively understand the same conducting gesture? Piotr Borkowski : I often wondered about that myself. A conducting gesture is not a language in the conventional sense. It has no vocabulary and no grammar. Yet musicians raised in completely different cultural environments instinctively understand it. Over time, I realized that performers do not respond to the movement itself. They respond to the intention carried within that movement. The gesture becomes a vessel for emotion, tension, serenity, dramatic intensity, lightness, or the natural breathing of a musical phrase. This invisible intention awakens the performer’s imagination and ultimately gives birth to sound. Gradually, that realization led me toward a broader reflection. The same principle extends far beyond musical performance. Great creators and exceptional interpreters become part of humanity’s lasting cultural heritage when they are able to touch something universal within human experience. Adrian Leonard Mociulschi: Then what gives a work of art the ability to survive the passage of time? Why do creators such as George Enescu continue to speak to successive generations long after their own era has passed? Piotr Borkowski: Talent and even genius are indispensable foundations, but they are not sufficient in themselves. What ultimately defines artistic greatness is the ability to express something profoundly true about the human condition. In conducting, intention is concealed within the gesture . In music, it lives within sound . In painting, it resides in colour and form . In literature, it is carried by words . The form itself is only the medium. What truly reaches us is the human intention embedded within the work. When that intention is genuine, it transcends language, history, and national borders. For this reason, I believe that time remains the most demanding critic, while successive generations become the most impartial jury . They are the ones who distinguish lasting works from those that merely enjoyed the fashion of their own age. Perhaps this is why George Enescu continues to live within European culture, not simply because he was a great Romanian composer, but because through the language of his own culture he expressed something profoundly true about what it means to be human. And whatever is genuinely true about humanity knows no borders. Adrian Leonard Mociulschi: If authenticity is essential to a work’s enduring value, how important is the role of people and institutions capable of recognising, supporting, and transmitting that value? Piotr Borkowski : Their role is absolutely fundamental. Throughout history, great artists have almost always been accompanied by people capable of recognising the value of their work. They were patrons, founders, publishers, educators, conductors, critics, festival organisers, and cultural visionaries. What united them was not merely an appreciation of beauty, but the imagination, courage, and responsibility required to recognise greatness before the rest of the world did. Today, many of those responsibilities belong to cultural institutions, ministries, foundations, festivals, competitions, orchestras, universities, and responsible media. Together they create the environment in which art can be created, preserved, and passed on to future generations. Their responsibility extends far beyond financial support. It lies in the ability to recognise enduring value. Without such discernment, even works of genius may remain unnoticed or disappear into obscurity. History repeatedly reminds us that the greatness of artists and the wisdom of enlightened patrons have always complemented one another. For this reason, I believe that the future of culture depends not only on those who create and perform, but equally on those who possess the vision to recognise authentic artistic value, nurture it, and ensure that it reaches future generations. Only when these two worlds, the artist and the enlightened guardian of culture, exist in harmony can great works transcend their own age and become part of humanity’s enduring memory. Adrian Leonard Mociulschi : Maestro Borkowski, thank you for sharing these reflections. As Bucharest welcomes a new generation of young musicians, your thoughts remind us that artistic greatness is measured not only by achievement, but by the ability to speak to humanity across time, cultures, and borders.
